_howTo: Edit any "text" freely. Keep "kind", "figure", "goal" and "options" as they are (they wire up the live figures). You can add, remove or reorder text blocks, and add or rename parts. Markup in text: **bold**, *italic*, [[words|colour]] to tie words to a figure colour (parcel = orange rising air, env = violet surrounding air, dew = teal dew point), and [^id] for a footnote. A footnote marker goes straight after the word or sentence it belongs to, with no space, and shows as a small raised number that opens a popup. Its note lives in "footnotes" at the end of the file under the same id, with a "kind" ("technical" for a term or detail, coloured teal, which also goes into the journal's glossary; "digression" for a side trip, coloured rose), a "title" and a "text". Add "glossary": false to keep a technical note out of the glossary, or a term ("glossary": "Radiosonde") to list it under that name. Numbers count up through the lesson by themselves. The lessons tell no story: the radio talks and the locals asking forecast questions (by forecast "id") are in data/radio.
title: Will this grey sky actually rain?
teaches: It’s dark and overcast: do you need an umbrella? Stable and unstable air, the lid that spreads heaps into dry stratocumulus, why depth and not darkness makes rain, and the soaking nimbostratus

blocks.title: The big ideas of this lesson
points: Nudge a bubble of air upward. In **stable** air it sinks back, like a weight on a spring; in **unstable** air it keeps rising, like a cork let go underwater.
An **inversion**, warmer air lying on cooler air, is a lid. Heaps rising under it spread into a lumpy grey sheet, **stratocumulus**, which looks gloomy but stays dry.
Darkness is a poor guide to rain. A raindrop holds about a million cloud droplets’ worth of water, and only a **deep** cloud gives drops time to grow that big.
A cloud holds only about 0.2 mm of water at any moment. Hours of soaking rain need a deep layer that is lifted, and refilled, for hours: **nimbostratus**, which hides the sun completely.

blocks.text: A grey sky is the commonest worry in forecasting. Some grey skies hang overhead all day and never drop a thing; others mean a soaking by lunch. Telling them apart takes two ideas: how the air behaves when it is nudged, and how deep the cloud is.

Why does air sometimes rise in isolated bubbles and other times stay in a flat layer? Suppose you give a parcel of air a small push upward. On some days, that parcel will keep rising on its own. On other days, it will sink right back down to where it started. Which way the atmosphere behaves on a given day determines almost everything about the clouds that form.

Air rises on its own when it is warmer than the air around it: a warm parcel is less dense than its neighbours, so the heavier air slides underneath and buoys it upward, like a hot-air balloon. A cold parcel is denser, and sinks.

While a rising dry parcel always cools at about 10 °C per kilometre, the [[air around it|env]] also changes temperature with height, and that surrounding profile varies from day to day. Averaged over the whole earth and year, the atmosphere gets colder by about 6.5 °C per kilometre of altitude.[^env-rate] On a hot afternoon when strong sunshine bakes the ground, the lowest kilometre or two can get colder with height by more than 10 °C per kilometre. On a clear morning after the ground has cooled all night, the temperature may drop much more slowly with height, or even get warmer as you go up: the **inversion** from Lesson 1.

To see what happens to a nudged parcel, compare the two cooling rates. Push a parcel up a kilometre, and it cools at 10 °C per kilometre on the way. If the surrounding air gets colder with height *faster* than that, say at 12 °C per kilometre, the parcel arrives at its new altitude warmer and less dense than its new neighbours. Because it is warmer and lighter, it keeps rising on its own, and the higher it climbs, the greater its temperature lead becomes. Meteorologists call this **unstable** air.

If instead the surrounding air gets colder with height *more slowly* than 10 °C per kilometre, say at 5 °C per kilometre, the nudged parcel arrives colder and denser than its new neighbours. Being heavier than the air around it, it sinks back down to where it started. That air is **stable**. Notice that stable and unstable describe the temperature profile of the surrounding sky on that day, which governs what happens to any parcel that gets nudged.

blocks.caption: Two days, two skies. Each bubble is nudged up one kilometre and cools 10 °C; what decides its fate is the air around it.

blocks.text: Here is a picture to hold on to: a weight on a spring versus a cork held underwater.

**Stable** air acts like a spring. Nudge a bubble of air upward, and it cools faster than the sky around it. Because cold air is dense and heavy, gravity pulls the chilled bubble right back down to where it started, just like a stretched spring snapping back to rest.

**Unstable** air is like a cork barely held at the bottom of a pool. Nudge a bubble upward, and it finds itself among air colder than itself, so buoyancy takes over. The slightest upward push releases it, and it shoots toward the surface faster and faster, stacking moisture into tall, billowing clouds rather than flat layers.
In the figure, the Air slider sets the sky around the bubble, and the picture beside it switches between the spring and the cork. The two temperatures beside the bubble tell you which one you have.

blocks.caption: A bubble of air nudged upward. Its own temperature is orange; the air around it is violet.
blocks.task: Nudge the bubble once in stable air and once in unstable air.

blocks.text: Those two behaviours give the sky its two basic textures. In unstable air, warm bubbles shoot up on their own wherever heated ground gives them a start, and each bubble builds its own cloud, forming **heaps**. In stable air, nothing climbs by itself. Air turns to cloud only if something does the cooling for it, to a whole layer at once: wind pushing the layer steadily up a mountain slope, or cold ground chilling the air resting on it. When a wide layer is cooled gently all together, it forms a flat **sheet**.

Nearly every cloud in the low sky is a heap, a sheet, or a mix of the two. You have met the pure sheet, stratus, and the pure heap, cumulus. The commonest mix of all is heaps that run into a stable layer and flatten out against it: the lumpy grey sheet that covers more of the earth than any other cloud.

Real skies often blend heaps and sheets together, and the most common cloud type on Earth is just such a hybrid: **stratocumulus**. At any given moment, stratocumulus decks cover roughly a fifth of the world’s oceans. Seen from below, stratocumulus looks like a broad layer of rounded lumps, rolls, or patches, darker grey in the thicker centres and brighter toward the edges, usually with small gaps of blue sky showing between the elements.

Stratocumulus forms underneath an **inversion**, a layer where the air gets warmer with height instead of colder. You saw an inversion in the first lesson when cold night air pooled on the valley floor; higher up in the sky, an inversion acts like a lid. Because atmospheric stability depends on the temperature profile of each specific layer, the air below the inversion can be well-mixed and unstable even while the inversion layer above it is strongly stable.

Beneath the lid, surface heating or wind turbulence stirs the air, sending buoyant bubbles upward that cool to their dew point and form cumulus heaps. As soon as a rising bubble pushes into the warm inversion layer, however, it finds itself colder and denser than the surrounding air and can climb no further. As more rising air continues to arrive from below, the cloud tops flatten and spread sideways against the underside of the lid. When the air is humid, the cloud base forms lower down and a deeper portion of each rising bubble condenses, supplying more cloud water to spread out laterally until neighbouring heaps press together into a continuous, lumpy sheet.

blocks.caption: Morning heaps rising under a layer of warmer air.
blocks.task: Strengthen the lid and add moisture until the heaps join into a sheet.

blocks.text: Stratus and stratocumulus are both low layers with fairly flat bases, so how do you tell them apart? By what made them, which shows in their texture. **Stratus** forms when a whole layer of stable air is cooled evenly: by a clear night, by moist air drifting over cold ground, or by fog lifting off a valley floor. Nothing stirs it, so it has no pattern at all, just one even, featureless grey sheet, often low enough to hide the hilltops.

**Stratocumulus** is built by stirring. Each rising bubble becomes a cell, thicker where the air rises in its middle and thinner where it sinks around its edges. From below, the layer breaks into lumps or rolls with darker centres, brighter rims, and often slits of blue between them. The bases of both are roughly flat; the difference is the pattern of light and shade across the underside.

blocks.caption: Two low layers, made two different ways.

blocks.text: The two often turn into each other. When the morning sun starts stirring a dawn stratus deck from below, it often breaks into the cells of stratocumulus before it burns away.

What creates an inversion lid a kilometre or two above the ground? Most often, it comes from air sinking slowly over a wide area. When air converges high in the atmosphere and gently subsides, the total weight of the air column increases, raising the barometric pressure at the ground in what forecasters call a **high-pressure system** (or simply a high). As that upper air sinks into higher pressure, it is compressed and warms at the dry rate of 10 °C per kilometre.

Meanwhile, the lowest kilometre or so of the atmosphere is constantly churned by wind and thermals rising off the ground. Any sinking air that reaches the top of this turbulent boundary layer[^boundary-layer] gets mixed in and carried back down and up by the eddies, so the large-scale sinking stops right at the top of the stirred layer. The compressed, warmed air from aloft therefore rests directly on top of cooler air mixed up from the surface, forming a sharp temperature inversion.

blocks.caption: Sinking air comes to rest on the stirred layer below, warmer on top of cooler.

blocks.text: Because the inversion lid is maintained by sinking air under high pressure and prevents clouds from growing tall, a sky covered in stratocumulus, however grey and overcast it looks, almost always brings dry, settled weather.

In the first lesson, you saw that typical cloud droplets are only about a hundredth of a millimetre across and settle at less than a centimetre per second, slow enough for the gentlest updraught to keep them suspended. Even if an individual cloud droplet drifts out the bottom of a cloud base, it enters drier air and evaporates within a few centimetres, long before reaching the ground.

A raindrop is vastly larger. A typical raindrop measures one to two millimetres across, or about a hundred times the diameter of a cloud droplet. Because the volume of a sphere grows with the cube of its diameter (100 × 100 × 100), a raindrop a hundred times wider contains a **million** times as much water. To produce a single raindrop that can survive the fall to the ground, roughly a million microscopic cloud droplets have to merge together.

blocks.caption: A hundred times wider holds a million times the water.
One drop leaving the base of a cloud, a kilometre above the wheat.
blocks.task: Find a drop that makes it all the way to the ground.

blocks.text: In clouds that are warmer than freezing from bottom to top, droplets grow by colliding and merging with one another.[^coalescence] A few droplets start out slightly larger than average, often because they condensed onto a larger particle such as a grain of sea salt. Larger droplets fall faster through the air. For droplets up to about a tenth of a millimetre across, fall speed increases with the square of the diameter (above that size, air resistance grows faster still and bends the curve over, as the fall-speed chart in the figure above shows).

A droplet that is five times wider than its neighbours therefore falls about twenty-five times faster, at several centimetres per second rather than a fraction of a centimetre per second. As it falls, it overtakes the smaller, slower droplets in its path and collides with them. Each merger makes the collector drop heavier and faster, allowing it to sweep through a wider column of cloud every second and accelerating its growth.

blocks.caption: A drop that gets ahead keeps getting further ahead.

blocks.text: Even so, this collision process takes tens of minutes, during which the growing drop is continuously falling. In a shallow cloud, the drop falls out the base long before it reaches raindrop size and evaporates on the way down. Only a deep cloud, or one with strong updraughts that hold the growing drops aloft, provides enough time for raindrops to mature. (In colder clouds that extend above the freezing level, ice crystals provide a second, faster pathway to rain, which Lesson 7 takes up.)

blocks.caption: The same start, in a thin cloud and a deep one.

blocks.text: That is why a cloud’s depth matters more than how dark it looks. Darkness is a poor guide on its own. A deeper cloud does let less light through, but so does a shallow one packed with a great many tiny droplets, and a crowd of tiny droplets is actually worse at making rain: the same water shared among more droplets leaves each one smaller and slower, so they rarely collide. (Smoke and field dust, which give water many more specks to condense on, make exactly such clouds.)[^ship-tracks]

Lighting fools the eye too. A cloud’s base always sits in its own shadow, and under a sheet that covers the whole sky there is nothing bright to compare it with. A thin grey layer can look gloomy all day and give no more than drizzle; rain needs a cloud with the depth, and the updraughts, to give its drops time to grow.

So how does a sky manage hours of steady rain? Start with how much water a cloud holds. Measured from aeroplanes, a layer of cloud carries about 0.2 grams of liquid water in each cubic metre: a fifth of a gram, spread through a space the size of a wardrobe. Picture a column of that cloud one kilometre deep standing on one square metre of ground: a thousand cubic metres, holding 200 grams of water. If every drop fell, it would cover the square metre 0.2 millimetres deep: about the thickness of two sheets of paper.

blocks.caption: Water on the ground, wrung out of the sky: from one cloud, one storm, and one year in the Columbia Basin, the dry country east of the Cascades.

blocks.text: A cloud, then, is not a full bucket that empties once. A long rain is more like a conveyor belt: the weather keeps lifting new moist air, cooling it, condensing it and raining it out, hour after hour, about a millimetre an hour on the rain gauge, while the cloud itself never holds more than its 0.2 mm.

blocks.caption: Moist air streams through a storm’s cloud and leaves its water behind as rain.

blocks.text: The cloud that runs that belt is **nimbostratus**: a dark, featureless grey layer several kilometres thick that produces hours of continuous rain or snow. It needs two things at once. It is a sheet, lifted gently and steadily over hundreds of kilometres, usually ahead of a front (Lesson 4 follows one coming), so the belt keeps running for hours. And it is deep, reaching from the low sky far up above the freezing level, where (as Lesson 7 shows) ice turns cloud water into snow that melts into rain on the way down.

In the naming system, *nimbo-* indicates a rain-bearing cloud rather than a specific altitude floor. The International Cloud Atlas puts nimbostratus on the middle floor, which the next lesson introduces, because its main body develops there, though it regularly thickens downward into the low floor. As rain falls out of the base into the air below, some of the drops evaporate, both cooling the sub-cloud air and adding water vapour to it. Before long, pockets of air beneath the main deck reach their dew point and condense into ragged, fast-moving shreds of low cloud known as **scud** (or pannus), making the dark base appear to sag toward the ridges.

From the ground, the quickest test is the sun. Under nimbostratus you cannot tell where the sun is at all; any thinner sheet lets you make it out, at least as a pale glow. The base is different too. Stratocumulus has a clear underside of lumps and rolls, lighter and darker patches; nimbostratus has a uniform, diffuse grey base that looks blurred and indistinct behind curtains of falling rain.

One more grey-sky sight is worth knowing. On a dry, warm day you may see grey streaks hanging from a high cloud base and fading out halfway to the ground. That is **virga**: rain or snow evaporating in the dry air below before it can land. It means the cloud is raining, but the ground will stay dry.

blocks.title: Will this grey sky rain?
points: Lumpy, with slits of blue, under a steady high: stratocumulus. Dry, or a spot of drizzle.
Flat, low and even, after a still night: stratus. Drizzle at most, and it usually burns off.
Deep and featureless, the sun gone without a trace, the base blurred into falling rain: nimbostratus. Hours of rain.
Streaks hanging from a high base that never reach the ground: virga. Dry below.

blocks.text: The drawings in this lesson are clean; real skies are not. Here are this lesson’s clouds in photographs, side by side with the clouds they are most often taken for, and the one thing that tells each pair apart. Keep these in mind for the check.

options.tell: Both are low grey sheets. Look for texture: lumps, rolls, or bright seams between darker patches make it stratocumulus. Grey that is even from edge to edge, like lifted fog, is stratus.
Look at the sky between them. Cumulus heaps stand apart with blue all round, and bulge upward. Stratocumulus lumps are spread flat and joined into one layer, with only gaps of sky.
Both are featureless grey. Nimbostratus is darker, being kilometres deep, and steady rain or snow falls from it. Stratus is a thin, paler lid low enough to hide hilltops, with drizzle at most.

blocks.text: First identify the cloud types in these photos, and then give your forecast for a few changing skies.

blocks.caption: The sky over a few hours. What is it up to?

items.question: Morning cumulus heaps spread into a lumpy grey sheet by afternoon. Will it rain this afternoon?
options: Yes: a grey sheet that thick will bring steady rain by evening
No: it will stay dry, with at most a spot of drizzle
Thunderstorms: heaps that spread out are building into towers
items.why: Cumulus heaps that flatten and spread beneath an inversion form stratocumulus. The inversion lid keeps the cloud layer shallow, so it stays dry or produces light drizzle at most.

items.question: Two grey layers: one thin but packed with tiny droplets, one twice as deep with fewer, bigger ones. The thin one looks darker. Which is likelier to rain?
options: The deep one: its drops have the depth and the size to grow into rain
The dark one: a darker cloud holds more water ready to fall as rain
Neither: a grey layer can only drizzle, however deep it grows
items.why: Darkness fools the eye: a shallow cloud packed with tiny droplets can look gloomier than a deep one. Rain needs drops to grow a million times bigger, and that takes depth and bigger droplets to start with.

items.question: A lumpy grey sheet with small gaps of blue has sat over the valley all day under high pressure. Will it bring a soaking rain?
options: Yes: a sheet that sits this long builds up water for hours of rain
Only if it lowers to the ground and turns into valley fog tonight
No: the lid keeps the layer too shallow to make real rain
items.why: Sinking air in a high-pressure system maintains a strong inversion lid that keeps stratocumulus shallow, and growing full-sized raindrops requires a deep cloud.

items.question: A grey sheet has thickened all morning until the sun is completely hidden and the base looks dark and blurred. What should you expect?
options: A brief passing shower, then sun again within the hour
Steady rain for several hours, from a deep, lifted layer
Nothing: the layer will thin out and burn off by midday
items.why: A deep, featureless grey deck that completely hides the sun and blurs into falling rain is nimbostratus. It is kept going by steady lifting, so it brings hours of rain, not a passing shower.

items.question: On a hot, dry afternoon, grey streaks hang from a high cloud base and fade away halfway down. Will the fields get wet?
options: Yes: the streaks are rain, and the rain is on its way down to you
Yes, but later: the streaks are building up for a downpour tonight
No: that is virga, rain evaporating in the dry air before it lands
items.why: Streaks that fade out below a high base are virga: the cloud is raining, but the dry air underneath evaporates every drop before it reaches the ground.

learned: Air is unstable when the surrounding air gets colder with height faster than a rising bubble cools (10 °C per kilometre in clear air); a nudged bubble keeps rising and builds heaps. In stable air the bubble sinks back, and cloud forms only as flat sheets, when a whole layer is lifted or chilled.

An inversion acts as a lid. Heaps rising under it spread into stratocumulus: a lumpy sheet with darker centres and slits of blue, often under the sinking air of a high, which looks grey but stays mostly dry.
A raindrop holds about a million cloud droplets’ worth of water; growing that big takes time and depth, so shallow clouds rarely rain however dark they look.
A cloud holds only about 0.2 mm of water at any moment; hours of rain need deep cloud that is lifted and refilled for hours, like a conveyor belt.
Nimbostratus is that cloud: deep, featureless, the sun hidden completely, its base blurred into falling rain. Streaks that never reach the ground are virga.

stability.title: Stable and unstable air
stability.text: A rising dry parcel cools at 10 °C per kilometre. If the surrounding air gets colder with height faster than that, a lifted parcel ends up warmer than its neighbours and keeps rising on its own; this is unstable air, which builds heaps. If the surrounding air cools more slowly with height, or warms with height in an inversion, a lifted parcel ends up colder than its neighbours and sinks back down; this is stable air, which turns to cloud only when a whole layer is cooled together into flat sheets.

stratocumulus.title: Stratocumulus
stratocumulus.text: A low layer of rounded lumps and rolls with darker grey centres and small gaps, formed when rising cumulus heaps flatten and spread beneath a stable temperature inversion. It is often capped by sinking air in a high-pressure system, bringing overcast but dry, settled weather. It is the most common cloud type on Earth.

rain.title: Why most clouds don’t rain
rain.text: Typical cloud droplets are about 0.01 mm across and settle at less than a centimetre per second. A raindrop is about a hundred times wider (1 to 2 mm), so its volume is roughly a million times larger. Larger droplets fall faster and sweep up smaller ones in their path, but only a deep cloud provides enough fall distance and time for droplets to grow into raindrops.

cloud-water.title: How much water a cloud holds
cloud-water.text: About 0.2 grams of liquid water in each cubic metre of a layer cloud: a kilometre of it, wrung out completely, would wet the ground 0.2 mm deep. A storm drops 10 to 15 mm in a day only because it keeps lifting new moist air and making new cloud for hours, like a conveyor belt, so a long rain needs a deep cloud that is lifted for a long time.

nimbostratus.title: Nimbostratus
nimbostratus.text: A dark, featureless grey cloud deck several kilometres deep that completely blots out the sun and produces hours of continuous rain or snow. It is lifted steadily over a wide area, usually ahead of a front, and reaches high above the freezing level, where ice turns its water into snow that melts into rain. Evaporating rain below its base often forms ragged shreds of low scud.

env-rate.title: Environmental lapse rate
env-rate.text: How fast the air around you cools with height is the **environmental lapse rate**, to set it apart from a parcel’s own rate. The 6.5 °C per kilometre average is built into the *standard atmosphere*, the made-up average sky that aeroplane altimeters are calibrated against. Weighing the two rates against each other is how forecasters judge stability.

boundary-layer.title: Boundary layer
boundary-layer.text: The **boundary layer** is the bottom of the atmosphere, the part that feels the ground: stirred by thermals and by wind dragging over the land by day, and calm, often cold, at night. On a sunny afternoon it can be one or two kilometres deep; on a clear night it may shrink to a hundred metres. Above it, the *free atmosphere* hardly knows what the ground is doing.

coalescence.title: Collision–coalescence
coalescence.text: Droplets merging as they bump is **coalescence**, and rain made this way comes by **collision–coalescence**, or *warm rain*, since no ice takes part. It is how most rain falls from shallow tropical clouds. Not every bump sticks: small droplets often bounce apart, or swerve around a bigger one in the air it pushes ahead of it.

ship-tracks.title: Ship tracks
ship-tracks.text: Satellite pictures of ocean stratocumulus sometimes show thin, bright lines hundreds of kilometres long, drawn across the grey. They are ship tracks: a ship’s exhaust adds specks to clean sea air, the same water is shared among more, smaller droplets, and that strip of cloud reflects more sunlight and drizzles less. When ships switched to cleaner fuel in 2020, most of the tracks faded.
